## My reasoning

I'm 75 now, and my knees aren't what they used to be. My two sons work in Handan city. I manage about 5 mu on my own — the same land my father farmed. I hire a tractor from the village cooperative for the big jobs because I can't do that myself anymore.

I grow winter wheat and summer corn — that's what everyone in Quzhou does, that's what I've done for 50 years, and I'm not changing. The wheat goes in the ground in October after I prep the field with the rotary. When the wheat comes off in June, I plant corn directly into the stubble — no need to plow again, saves my back and saves money on diesel. The corn is out by September and then I start again.

For wheat seeds I buy the improved variety from the village supply station — the one the township extension office has been selling for the past few years. It's not the fanciest new seed but it works on my soil. For corn I always buy hybrid seed — even I know that's worth the extra money.

Fertilizer: I put down compound fertilizer as a base before wheat planting, then I top-dress with urea at jointing. I know some younger farmers say I'm using too much, but I'd rather have the yield be safe. I do the same for corn — compound base when I plant, urea when the plants are knee-high.

Irrigation: wheat needs four waterings here in Hebei — I do the sowing water, the overwintering water before it freezes, the jointing water, and the grain-fill water. For corn I usually only water twice unless it's a dry year — once when I plant and once when it tassels.

Pesticides: I spray herbicide on the wheat in spring and something for the aphids before heading. For corn I usually just spray once if I see pests — most years it's not too bad.

I expect about 400 jin per mu for wheat and around 1100 jin per mu for corn if the weather holds. That's been my average.
